text: A psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I lack nothing.
He lets me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters.
He restores my soul. He guides me along right paths for his name's sake.

Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,* I fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. [*Footnote: Or "the darkest valley"; the Hebrew word can mean deep darkness as well as the shadow of death.]

versions.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
versions.explanation: The rendering is well established and reads well aloud, but the Hebrew term (tsalmavet) is commonly understood as "deep darkness." A brief footnote would inform readers without disturbing the familiar cadence.

text: You set a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.
Surely goodness and mercy will pursue me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for length of days.* [*Footnote: Or "as long as I live."]

versions.text: Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD as long as I live.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb is stronger than "follow"—it means to pursue or chase after—and the closing phrase literally reads "for length of days," which leaves room for the psalm's open-ended hope; "as long as I live" narrows it. Placing the interpretive rendering in a footnote preserves both sense and rhythm.
